title: Smart glasses banned from Melbourne council's pools, gyms and playgrounds
text:
An inner Melbourne council has voted to ban smart glasses from its pools, gyms, playgrounds and childcare centres due to concerns about vulnerable members of the community being covertly filmed.

The City of Yarra last night voted to ban glasses with in-built cameras from its facilities as well as lobby the federal government to update the Privacy Act to respond to the risks posed by new wearable technologies.

There will be exceptions for users who are hearing impaired, have low vision or other disabilities who are aided by smart glasses.

Yarra councillor Sophie Wade forwarded the motion and said she was particularly worried about children, women and LGBTQI+ people being filmed without their knowledge.

"These glasses are pretty cheap and lots of people could have them very soon," she told the meeting.

Smart glasses have been available for several years but privacy concerns have grown as cheaper versions arrived on the market for less than $100.

Smart glasses will be banned from City of Yarra-run childcare centres. (Supplied: City of Yarra)

The federal government recently signalled that local councils would be responsible for governing the wearable technology after saying it had no plans to ban imports of smart glasses.

Yarra councillor Andrew Davies said he would not normally support a motion that shifted more responsibility and cost onto local governments.

"But Cr Wade's got a really good point and we need to do something," he said.

" The fact that we need to protect children and women in particular from perverts — let's just say it — is really important. "

Yarra mayor Stephen Jolly said he believed the municipality was only the second council in Australia to implement the ban, after Brisbane City Council last month announced a city-wide ban on smart glasses at its public pools.

"We don't trust the tech bros to do it and the federal government, unfortunately, haven't brought in legislation on this matter," Cr Jolly said.

Melburnians swim and enjoy the sun at the Fitzroy Swimming Pool. (ABC News: Margaret Burin )

He said the ban would be enforced within days.

"In the wrong hands, in those environments where there's public toilets, lots of kids hanging around, people swimming, they can be misused," Cr Jolly said.

"Because of the lack of control over these glasses by the federal or state governments, councils have had to step up."

Federal Attorney General Michelle Rowland last week acknowledged community concerns about smart glasses and said she was not ruling out taking other steps to address the risks.

Greens want 12-month ban on wearable devices

Yarra councillor Evangeline Aston voted against the motion.

Cr Aston said she "absolutely" supported the need to protect the community but she did not want council to lobby the federal government to play its part.

"The government has a strong track record of developing terrible legislation when it comes to technology and I simply think we are in a better position to design things for our own local context," she told the meeting.

She also added that she was not interested in using the council to advance federal Greens party policies.

The ban aims to stop people being filmed with smart glasses without their knowledge. (ABC News: Shaun Kingma)

The Greens announced last month they would push to ban camera-enabled wearable devices for one year while urgent updates to the Privacy Act were made.

"These covert wearables are a disturbing technology," said senator David Shoebridge.

"They're built to let someone film you without your knowledge in a change room, on the street, or at your kid's swimming lesson, and our law does nothing about it," Senator Shoebridge said.

"Australia's privacy laws were written four decades before this technology existed, and every day we wait is another day these devices fly off the shelves with no rules attached."

The Richmond Recreation Centre is one of the facilities where smart glasses will be banned. (Supplied: City of Yarra)

Cr Aston and Meca Ho were the only two Yarra councillors to vote against the motion.

Cr Jolly said it was "ridiculous" that councils had to take carriage of the issue.

"It's like saying, 'there's no national seatbelt law', so a council has to say that 'if you're driving around Yarra you've got to wear a seatbelt'," he said.

"But maybe we can put the pressure on here by a large council like Brisbane and a smaller council like Yarra in Melbourne, maybe we can start a bit of a trend."

title: Major state fears cricket will be worse off with private investment
text:
The decision to introduce private investment into the Big Bash leagues risks leaving cricket in Australia "strategically and financially worse off", according to Cricket NSW.

On Tuesday, Cricket Australia announced it would seek private investment into Australia's franchise T20 leagues, beginning with the sale of the Melbourne Renegades.

The announcement came following months of speculation about whether private investment was the right move for CA, and the game in Australia more broadly.

Private investment in Big Bash Cricket Australia agrees to bring private investment into the Big Bash League, starting with the sale of the Melbourne Renegades.

Ahead of Tuesday's announcement, it was reported that state cricket bodies in NSW and Queensland were opposed to the plan which included exploring sell-offs of 49 per cent stakes in BBL franchises.

On Wednesday, Cricket NSW in a statement said it was disappointed Cricket Australia had pushed forward with the decision to seek private investment without having all stakeholders on board with the process.

"Cricket NSW is disappointed by Cricket Australia's decision to proceed with introducing private investment into the Big Bash leagues without alignment across Australian cricket," the statement read.

"This decision risks leaving cricket in NSW and Australia strategically and financially worse off, with direct consequences for our ability to invest in grassroots cricket.

"We see our role at Cricket NSW, alongside Cricket Australia and all states, as custodians of our game. Our purpose is to inspire everyone to play and love cricket. This starts with growing participation in our sport, ultimately producing great players for our W/BBL clubs, NSW and Australia.



"The profits from our successful and healthy Big Bash clubs – the Sydney Sixers and Sydney Thunder – are reinvested into growing participation in cricket."

Cricket NSW owns the Sydney Sixers and Sydney Thunder franchises.

It said it feared the private investment model would threaten its ability to invest in growing the sport, especially at the grassroots level.

Cricket Australia green lights BBL privatisation The Big Bash League is set to look like it never has before as Cricket Australia prepares to welcome private ownership to the competition.

"Yesterday’s announcement threatens this system. The redistribution of profits to external investors reduces our ability to invest in community cricket, creating long-term impacts at all levels," Cricket NSW said.



"The Cricket NSW board is also disappointed by the process leading to this decision.

"We have raised concerns directly with Cricket Australia, proposed an alternative pathway to strengthen the Big Bash, and highlighted significant risks within the proposal, informed by high-quality external advice."

On Tuesday, Cricket Australia chair Mike Baird said the introduction of private investment into the Big Bash would result in greater investment in the sport at all levels.

"By opening the door to private investment in the Big Bash leagues, Cricket Australia is taking a deliberate step to strengthen and secure the long-term future of the game, accelerate growth and ensuring we can keep investing in community cricket and grassroots participation, domestic and international pathways and the elite level," he said.

"This is a significant decision that has involved an enormous amount of analysis, discussion and collaboration over many months. I'd like to thank all involved as we move to what we believe is the best way to secure cricket's future in this country, strengthen the Big Bash and protect our standing on the global stage."

Cricket Australia is hopeful that the Melbourne Renegades franchise will play the 2027/28 season under new ownership.

title: Clydesdale who pulled historic horse-drawn tram remembered as gentle giant
text:
One of the Clydesdales of the Victor Harbor Horse-Drawn Tram has died after a short illness.

In a statement released yesterday, staff at the Victor Harbor Tramway said Albert, an 18-year-old strawberry roan gelding, had died on Saturday after becoming ill on Friday.

Albert had been part of the tramway team for 13 years. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

Veterinarians have confirmed that tumours were the cause of his illness and death.

Albert had been part of the team that pulls the historic horse-drawn tram from Victor Harbor to Granite Island for 13 years.

At 17.3 hands high, he was one of the tallest members of the tramway's herd and was often used to help train new horses and drivers due to his calm nature.

Meg Whibley, general manager of the Victor Harbor Horse Drawn Tram Authority, said Albert was her "go-to" horse when it came to training new staff.

"He was very forgiving," she said.

"We just trusted him in so many ways."

Albert is also being remembered for his unique personality.

Meg Whibley, the manager of the Victor Harbor Horse-Drawn Tram, seen here with Albert. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

Unlike most of the team, he disliked wearing blinkers, preferring to see everything around him as he made the 650-metre causeway crossing between Victor Harbor and Granite Island.

However, he always regarded fishermen along the causeway and their rods and buckets with suspicion.

"He'd just look as if to say, 'No, we need to get past here,'" said Britt Jablonski, the tramway's head trainer.

Albert's best mate, Murray, is getting special attention at the moment. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

Albert was named after the nearby Lake Albert and was described as being best friends with fellow tramway horse Murray, with the two often seen grazing and sharing hay together in the tramway's large paddocks just outside Victor Harbor.

Ms Whibley said, since Albert's death Murray had been getting special attention and had been paired up with another of the authority's horses so he did not get too lonely.

The community has been asked to be mindful of the impact of Albert's death on the staff and volunteers of the tramway.

Albert pulling a special sunrise tram service in January 2026. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

It comes after a difficult period for the tramway, which was forced to stop running because of a mystery flu-like illness in some of its other horses in April and May, as well as reduced income in recent years due to the impact of South Australia's algal bloom.

title: The departing Panther who shapes as Penrith's finals wildcard
text:
Jack Cole's chance on the NRL's biggest stage has been a long time coming, but now the Penrith five-eighth could shape as the Panthers finals wildcard.

Sunday's semi-final against the Sydney Roosters will be just his fifth game of the year and 22nd of his career since his debut four years ago.

Cole has spent the time since in and out of first grade, and while the 23-year old was always part of the team he only sporadically strapped up on match day, especially as the season heated up.

For four straight Septembers, Cole ran opposed sessions and tried to do whatever else he could to get the top side ready for whatever finals battle was to come, waiting for his chance as he bore witness to the greatest dynasty of modern times.

Cole has started at five-eighth in Penrith's last two matches of the regular season. (Getty Images: Matt King)

It was not always easy to be patient, but now, at the very end of his Panthers tenure before he joins Perth Bears next season, Cole's time has come.

The Orange man signed with the Bears to try and be a first grader every week, now he is a first grader in one of the weeks that counts the most.

"The last few years, watching the boys kick on and win grand finals, you try and help where you can," Cole said.

"But it's a different perspective now — going on the camps, being in the meetings, it's a good opportunity and I'm really looking forward to it.

"It has been a little bit [hard to wait]. There's been a few soft tissue injuries over the past couple of years as well, that's been more frustrating. You get close, you have an injury, and you need to work your way back up.

"It's all been character building though. I haven't had it the easy way, I've gone up and come down and known what I've had to work on and tried to work my way back up."

Cole's combination with Cleary will prove crucial for Penrith in their finals tilt. (Getty Images: Ethan Miller)

Cole has spent some time under the bright lights. He got a start in the World Club Challenge against Wigan in 2024 and began last season as the team's starting five-eighth, including in the win over Cronulla in Las Vegas.

Chances have been harder to come by since, but Blaize Talagi's demotion to reserve grade and Jack Cogger's three-game suspension for a high tackle opened the door for Cole.

He has also combined well with Nathan Cleary as Penrith warmed up for the finals with back-to-back wins.

"He's [Cogger] had a few [suspensions] this year, so we thought he might get suspended and I didn't know if Ivan [Cleary] would go Blaize or me or someone else. But it was definitely something I started thinking about straight away," Cole said.

"[Cleary] just said to me to defend well and if I see something attack, just do it.

"He wants me to keep it simple, do my role and the rest will fall into place."

With the best player in the world on his inside and lethal centre-wing duo Casey McLean and Thomas Jenkins on his left, Cole's job is a simple one — take a little pressure off Cleary when he can, shuffle it out to the weapons early and often, always keep talking and tackle well.

But simple is not the same as easy. If it were, Penrith would not have made the change with Talagi in the first place.

After signing with Penrith as a 15-year old, Cole will head to Perth Bears at the end of the season. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

Cogger is due to return from suspension for the Panthers next match, but it feels like there is every chance Cole sticks around in one spot or another.

Throughout Penrith's ascension and well into their dynasty, coach Cleary has a great tradition of shaking up his side on the eve of the finals to give it a little extra juice.

In 2021 he benched talismanic backrower Viliame Kikau for Liam Martin for the final six games of the season.

The following year Cleary did the same, only with hookers Api Koroisau and Mitch Kenny, in the club's three finals games.

In 2023 it was Cogger who seized a bench utility spot for the preliminary final and the decider, a move which paid off handsomely when he played a key role in Penrith's epic comeback against Brisbane.

How this unlikely hero set the stage for Nathan Cleary's grand final heroics Nathan Cleary is rightly earning all sorts of praise for his grand final performance but the Penrith halfback couldn't have spearheaded his side's remarkable comeback without the efforts of Jack Cogger.

Paul Alamoti has been the choice two years in a row. In 2024 he replaced Casey McLean at left centre for the final five games of the season and ended up scoring the final try of the grand final win over Melbourne.

Last year he came in for Tom Jenkins on the wing for the semis, scoring five tries in three games leading up to the preliminary final loss to Brisbane.

If all goes well on Sunday, Cole could be this year's version of the late-season adrenaline shot which has worked so well for the Panthers for so many years.

Cogger's proven ability to impact a game off the bench could keep Cole in the starting side, or Cole himself could act as the club's utility given he can also cover centre.

But we are getting ahead of ourselves, which Cole refuses to do. Big dreams about a grand final exit before he heads to Perth will have to wait.

Cole has been with the Panthers since he was 15 and is determined to put into practice everything he has learned since, first on Sunday and then with whatever comes next.

"When it was first happening [getting to the end] I was a bit sad cause I only had six or seven games left and I've been here for eight years," Cole said.

"But now there's a job to do and I can't dwell on that. It won't benefit me or the team.

"I want to use it as an opportunity to help me moving forward and hopefully end on a good note.

"This is the time of year you wait for. This is what it's all about."

title: Visitor tax on short-stay accommodation dies in Tasmanian parliament
text:
A Tasmanian government push to introduce a visitor tax on short-stay accommodation has been defeated in the state's upper house, with Labor and multiple independents voting it down.

The short-stay levy was a 2024 election promise and was supposed to partially pay for the two-year exemption on stamp duty offered to first home buyers.

That exemption has now ended, and the government says it would have been reinvested into housing initiatives.

Initial estimates from the government were that the levy would raise about $11 million per year, but the government revised that figure to $8 million after amendments.

Abetz chastises levy opponents

Tasmanian short-stay numbers jump amid rental squeeze Almost 500 more whole homes in Tasmania have been converted to short-stay accommodation in just over a year.

In a statement, Treasurer Eric Abetz accused Labor of "hypocrisy".

"The Tasmanian government's modest 5 per cent short stay levy, which would have been paid for overwhelmingly (over 80 per cent) by interstate and international visitors, has been voted down by Labor," he said.

​"The Tasmanian government took this commitment to the election. It has been consulted on over years. It had strong protections for hotels, motels, inns and other similar commercial accommodation.

​"Labor voted against it. Labor's choice for treasurer, Ruth Forrest, voted against it. They cannot have it both ways: calling for fiscal responsibility then voting down sensible revenue measures which would have supported first home buyers paid for by non-Tasmanians.

​"Their hypocrisy is writ large and Tasmanians are understandably disappointed."

Eric Abetz attacked opponents of the levy. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Few were complimentary about the bill during the debate, including those who ultimately supported it.

Labor MP Luke Edmunds said the bill was not fit for purpose and "doesn't contribute to solving the rental crisis or housing affordability".

"This bill would levy money from the regions and spend it on first home owner schemes known to perpetuate the housing affordability problem by amplifying demand but not supply," he said.

He called on the government to "consult properly, do some modelling and bring back a policy that actually improves housing outcomes".

"As others have said, I think this policy is risky and poorly thought out. It's detrimental to tourism in our regions and it already has many unintended consequences.

" I'm opposing the short-stay levy because it raises a tax, not a housing solution. "

Greens MLC Cassy O'Connor said she recognised that it was "highly political" and "that it will do very little, if anything, to ease the reality of the housing crisis, the availability of affordable housing".

But she said the Greens would support it as a revenue-raising measure.

"We recognise that this is the government pretending that it's doing something to rein in short-stay accommodation, an issue that they've failed to get on top of ever since it surfaced in Tasmania, an issue that they have abandoned councils on as well," she said.

"But we made the decision to support this bill because it is a revenue-raising measure and, at the moment, the state needs to raise all the revenue that it can and to make all the efficiencies that it can without impacting on the delivery of services in Tasmania."

(Supplied)

Independent for Murchison Ruth Forrest told parliament she had initially welcomed the government's promise because it would raise money for the state.

"We've got a real budgetary problem here, we need to raise revenue and thank God they're actually looking at a new tax. And it is a tax, let's face it," she said.

"Members will be well familiar with my consistent position on the state's fiscal position.

"Tasmania's own-source revenue as a share of total expenditure is at historic lows. Treasury, in their fiscal sustainability report of 2026, made it really clear: we need to pull all three levers, and one of them is raising revenue.

" So, a big tick for that in a policy sense, not necessarily a practical sense. "

Ruth Forrest voted against the levy. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

But she said she was concerned about a lack of modelling, how much of the tax would ultimately be on Tasmanians and where the money was being directed.

"This won't fix the housing crisis. It won't," she said.

In the end, Ms Forrest voted against the levy.

Independent for Nelson Meg Webb said there was an "incontrovertible lack of clarity about the intent of this bill".

"The intent was to win votes, so it just needed to sound good as a media grab and bite on the day," she said.

"It just needed to sound like it might be something that appealed to average Tasmanians out in the street as a reasonable thing to do. It had to present well as a social media tile, or grab."

And like many others, Ms Webb was concerned about the fact it was unlikely to address the housing issue.

"My wish would be that we would be talking about a piece of legislation and policy that was there to deliver an improvement in our absolutely catastrophic housing crisis in this state," she said.

"We see a race to the top of rents because of excessively low vacancy rates that are so far below market failure, it's a joke really but it's not a joke because it's people's lives, it's people's wellbeing and health and livelihoods and access to a reasonable life in this state that is the victim of this situation we find ourselves in."

'A bit of a hot mess'

The Upper House's newest member, Independent for Huon Clare Glade-Wright, said that as the cost would be borne by the visitor, not the homeowner, there was "no apparent disincentive for whole homestay conversions".

"We need to make sure the policy instrument matches the policy objective, so we need to be really clear that this is a revenue-raising measure designed to raise funds from visitors and direct those funds towards first homeowner grants," she said.

While she raised multiple concerns, Ms Glade-Wright ultimately voted for the bill.

"This bill is clearly a bit of a hot mess but … it's a starting point with some of the tweaks by the amendments … and with the review in place, I think that gives an opportunity to work out if the revenue-raising instrument is actually doing what it's hoping to do and to perhaps consider directing funds towards housing supply in the future," she said.

The final vote was six to six, with the president using his casting vote to vote it down, as is convention.

Clare Glade-Wright also voted against the levy. (Facebook: Clare Glade-Wright)

Upon its defeat, Labor shadow treasurer Dean Winter celebrated the "collapse" of Mr Abetz's "confused tourism tax".

"Instead of delivering a clear and coherent strategy to fix Tasmania's housing crisis, the Liberals cooked up legislation so riddled with contradictions that even the upper house couldn't save it," he said.

"This policy was a complete mess. The government tried to claim the tourism tax wouldn't hurt everyday Tasmanians or local operators, yet the legislation was so confused it left the entire sector baffled.

"When a Treasurer brings a tourism tax bill to Parliament with no economic modelling, no clear operational logic, and no idea how it impacts the broader economy, this is the result."

title: Six new AI data centres proposed for Tasmania, but who by is being kept secret
text:
Unnamed companies are looking at setting up six data centres in Tasmania, a document tabled by the state government in parliament reveals.

Two of the six "confidential" projects are in the feasibility stage, meaning a preferred site has been selected and the proponents are undergoing further assessments to determine overall feasibility.

One of those is listed as needing 200-300 megawatts (MW) of energy, which could make it the biggest data centre in the state, depending what end of the range it sits at.

That facility is proposed for the state's north-west.

Another listed project would also use 200-300 MW, though is still in the concept stage.

The document states a 50 MW project in the concept stage had "expressed interest" in the closed manganese smelter in northern Tasmania, Liberty Bell Bay.

If the six confidential projects proceed, they would use at least 500 MW of power.

The state government would not confirm if the six proposals were from one company or multiple.

These proposals are in addition to Firmus Technologies' three AI data centres in Tasmania — one under construction in Launceston, another approved for construction in the Bell Bay Advanced Manufacturing Zone, and another waiting for approval at Wesley Vale in the state's north-west.

Firmus is on track to become the state's biggest power user, with its three facilities needing a combined 444 MW.

Firmus confirmed it was not behind the six new proposals.

VIRIDIS is also setting up a small 1 MW data centre in Burnie, and has council approval.

Greens accuse premier of 'keeping Tasmanians in the dark'

The document's release comes after the Greens moved a motion calling on the state government to table "details of all proposed AI data proponents working with the Office of the Coordinator General [OCG], their locations, and estimated power and water construction" by September 8.

Tasmania's coordinator general is a government position which aims to attract and support investment in the state.

Premier Jeremy Rockliff alongside Firmus co-CEOs Tim Rosenfield and Oliver Curtis at their Launceston facility. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

The document states the OCG had supported some of the proponents in site identification and stakeholder engagement, as well as facilitated introductions to existing and proposed energy developers.

Regarding the confidentiality of much of the details, the document states the OCG's conversations with proponents often occur at a preliminary stage and may involve commercial sensitive information.

"Where information has not been included, this reflects that it is either not yet available, not sufficiently settled, not capable of reliable estimation, or has been provided to OCG in confidence," the document states.

" This is not intended to limit the parliament's access to information, but to ensure the information provided is accurate, appropriately qualified and does not compromise current or prospective commercial processes. "

Rosalie Woodruff has accused the government of not being transparent around AI data centres in Tasmania. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

In parliament, Greens leader Rosalie Woodruff accused Premier Jeremy Rockliff of "actively keeping Tasmanians in the dark about your government's involvement in AI data centre developments".

"Under Greens and community pressure on Monday, you released a draft non-binding statement of expectations, and it has no guardrails for the largest ever resource bonanza in Tasmania's history.

" Why are you selling Tasmania's energy and water resources to AI data centre giants without asking Tasmanians what they want, before you've even established your own expectations? "

The government has released a Statement of Expectations for Data Centres and AI Infrastructure for public consultation.

Mr Rockliff accused the Greens of trying to "scare" the public.

He said his government expected transparency from data centre proponents, but that the sector would create jobs for Tasmanians.

"We understand very clearly that we want to know more about these projects and Tasmanians want to know more about these projects, and that's entirely reasonable, we acknowledge that," he said.

" It's also very important to recognise that data centres represent exactly the kind of investment that Tasmania should be attracting. "

Latrobe council sends Firmus project to government

Latrobe council has received a development application from Firmus for a 52 MW AI data centre in Wesley Vale.

On Monday night, the council decided to formally ask Planning Minister Kerry Vincent to assess it as a major project, meaning the council would not need to assess it.

Firmus is proposing an AI data centre at the site of the old paper mill at Mill Park in Wesley Vale. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

It also requested amendments to the planning scheme, which Mayor Peter Freshney said was "not fit for purpose" to appropriately consider data centre proposals.

"Those concerns from the community and others in the sector cannot be addressed to the extent they need to be under the current framework," Cr Freshney told ABC Northern Tasmania.

He said while there could be positives to data centre developments for the local and state economy, the planning scheme did not allow councils to consider all the relevant matters.

"The application will need to be considered to weigh up the risks and ensure we don't have legacy issues caused by failure to properly and appropriately assess these applications in a framework that is fit for purpose," he said.

title: Socceroo Cristian Volpato's fate uncertain after failed cocaine test
text:
Cristian Volpato's immediate availability for the Socceroos rests in the hands of Football Australia after NSW Police confirmed the World Cup star had tested positive for cocaine on a secondary test.

Volpato was pulled over by police on Sydney's Anzac Bridge on July 24 and returned a positive roadside reading for cocaine.

The 22-year-old then underwent independent testing at a private clinic, where it was claimed he returned a negative reading.

Police catch Socceroos star Police say they stopped the 22-year-old in a BMW Coupe about 1am today and allege he was travelling 109 kilometres per hour on the Anzac Bridge.

But Volpato was then sent for a secondary oral fluid test by police, which again confirmed a positive result for cocaine.

"On Tuesday 1 September 2026, a 22-year-old man was issued a Traffic Infringement Notice for drive motor vehicle with illicit drug present in oral fluid," NSW Police told AAP.

Volpato, who will face no further action, was handed a $722 fine as a result of the second positive test.

The Sassuolo forward had been pulled over by police after driving at 109 kilometres per hour in a 60km/h zone.

The Sydney-born youngster was a late inclusion for the Socceroos' World Cup campaign after switching his international allegiance from Italy to Australia on the eve of the tournament.

Volpato has maintained his innocence over the failed drugs test when he spoke to Football Australia (FA) staff, insisting that he never knowingly ingested the substance.

He also undertook a test when he returned to Italy which was negative, his club side, Sassuolo, said.

In a statement provided to AAP, Football Australia (FA) said: "Football Australia has been made aware of information concerning a reported secondary oral test result relating to one of our players. We are currently seeking independent verification.

"The matter is being managed in accordance with Football Australia's established protocols. To protect the integrity of this process and ensure procedural fairness, we will not comment further."

But the positive reading on Volpato's secondary police test could have major ramifications for his availability heading into January's Asian Cup.

Sources have told AAP that Volpato could be hauled before FA's disciplinary and ethics committee, where the sport's governing body has the power to suspend him from national team action.

The closest comparable case to Volpato's is that of A-League Women goalkeeper Teresa Morrissey, who tested positive for cannabis while driving.

Morrissey claimed the cannabis had been used for medicinal purposes, but was still slugged with a three-game ban by FA last year, which the goalkeeper's legal team had argued was disproportionate with her public profile.

Volpato's off-field indiscretion attracted headlines in Australia and in Italy, where he plays in Serie A.

Popovic knocked back extension Socceroos coach Tony Popovic has revealed he turned down a four-year contract offer from Football Australia (FA) to take the team through to the 2030 World Cup.

He has played three games for Sassuolo this season, but failed to finish their last game against Bologna because of a suspected hamstring injury.

Socceroos coach Tony Popovic would not be drawn on whether he would pick Volpato for this month's friendlies with Brazil when he spoke at a press conference in Sydney on Tuesday.

"I don't know exactly the details of what happened and it would be wrong to speculate on what happened," Popovic told reporters.

"These young men, things happen and you can get caught for something we have to look into.

"There is a process that's playing out at the moment and we need to follow that process.

"When that is played out as it should, [only] then I can really comment on that."

AAP

title: 'Darwin is a small place': NT deputy chief defends data centre disclosure
text:
The Northern Territory's deputy chief minister has defended his decision not to publicly disclose a potential conflict of interest with a close family member, saying "the rules are what they are" and he has followed them "to a T".

The ABC reported yesterday that Gerard Maley had appeared at a press conference spruiking a deal with Beetaloo Energy to build a $40 billion data centre outside Darwin, without revealing his sister-in-law, Bethaney Maley, worked for the firm in a "strategic engagement" role.

The "do not deal" agreement announced in July gives Beetaloo Digital exclusive rights over the land for a year, granting the company time to secure investors and work out whether the hyperscale data centre project is viable.

Mr Maley was not required to disclose the potential conflict on his public register of interests and told ABC Radio Darwin this morning he had informed Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro, despite not believing any conflict existed.

Beetaloo Energy chief executive Alex Underwood shakes hands with Gerard Maley at the press conference in which Lands Minister Josh Burgoyne (left) announced the agreement. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

"Darwin is a small place, there's three generations of Maleys here in the NT, you don't just pop out of a genie bottle when you become a politician and go back in when you finish that," he said.

"This 'do not deal' is a block of land that Minister Burgoyne did, there's a one-year deal on it so I don't think there's a conflict of interest and in any case, I've disclosed all the rules as I'm meant to do."

Mr Maley said Ms Maley was there "handing out press packs" at the announcement, so their connection was out in the open, and he blamed reporters for not raising this at the time.

Gerard Maley says Bethaney Maley is "an expert in the field" and "all the reporters know her". (Supplied)

"I think it's a bit rich for people to say you haven't declared it publicly," he said.

"She was there, your reporters were there, if they wanted to cry wolf they should have back then, but she was there and what more can you do?

"All the reporters know her, she's been around, she's an expert in the field, what more can you do in those sort of situations?"

Outside of the Beetaloo project, corporate records show that Mr Maley and Ms Maley have business ties, with both listed as shareholders for company Ammarula Pty Ltd, along with Ms Maley's husband — Gerard Maley's brother — Peter Maley.

Mr Maley said the decision to enter the "do not deal" agreement was made by Lands Minister Joshua Burgoyne and he was only there "to promote mines and energy in the NT".

"We know that mines and energy pay for things in the NT, they even pay for the ABC, the taxpayer funded [services], they pay for the education system, they pay for the police," he said.

"We need to make sure that we promote mining and gas in the NT so we can stand alone here in the NT and have a better lifestyle."

Gerard Maley says he will exclude himself from "any potential conflict of interest in relation to anything in relation to the NT". (ABC News: Dane Hirst )

Mr Maley said he had no involvement in Mr Burgoyne's decision and would continue to "follow the rules" where "I believe there's a conflict or a perceived conflict" in any cabinet discussions going forward.

"I'm not going to talk about cabinet and how cabinet works, that's a confidential process, but what I can say is I can assure Territorians that I will follow the rules, I will follow the guidelines and I will always act in the best interests of the NT," he said.

"I'll exclude myself from any potential conflict of interest in relation to anything in relation to the NT because I think the Territory's worth fighting for and that's what I'm here to do."

'Serious questions'

Labor Opposition MLA Dheran Young said constituents in his electorate of Daly, where the data centre would be built if the plans come to fruition, will have concerns about a lack of transparency.

"Many Territorians, and particularly people in the rural area, will have questions about this," he said.

Dheran Young says there has been "no consultation to date" about the proposed hyperscale data centre. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"We've seen this agreement signed with Beetaloo Energy, it's now been revealed [Mr Maley] has a family member that works for Beetaloo Energy.

"So I think it will have some serious questions, because there has been no consultation to date from the CLP [Country Liberal Party] government about this hyperscale AI data centre."

Independent MLA Justine Davis said Mr Maley "absolutely needs to be transparent about what conversations are happening" between himself and Beetaloo Digital.

Justine Davis says the news of Gerard Maley's family link at Beetaloo Digital could create a "public trust" issue. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"Because trust in government is all about actually trusting that they are acting in your interest," she said.

" It's just not good enough to have someone who's the deputy chief minister having a close relative in a senior role in a company that is going to be benefiting from the deals that this government's signing off on. "

Data centre 'a great opportunity'

NT deputy chief minister's family link to $40b data centre company plans The NT deputy chief minister has been spruiking a gas company granted rights to 185 hectares of government land to build a data centre, despite his sister-in-law working for the firm.

Environment Centre NT acting director Bree Ahrens said her organisation had been "shocked" and "really disappointed" by the revelation.

"It's not because there is any evidence that Minister Maley has failed to make the required disclosures but it's a broader issue of public trust and public confidence in the government," she said.

But Master Builders NT chief executive Sallyann Innes said her industry wanted and needed the work that would come from the construction of data centres.

"We need a long-term transparent pipeline of work, policies that encourage business investment, and this is a great opportunity," she said.

"But also it helps with our workforce development and maintaining that skilled workforce here in the NT."

title: Opal readers to be turned off on Sydney Ferries amid industrial action
text:
Opal card readers on Sydney ferries will be turned off for almost four weeks, the maritime workers union says as they step up industrial action against the private operator Transdev.

Sydney Ferries workers have been stuck in enterprise bargaining negotiations with the operator, as the Maritime Union of Australia (MUA) pushes for a 5 per cent wage increase and an annual increase to offset inflation.

MUA deputy branch secretary Paul Garrett told 702 ABC Sydney the card readers will be turned off from 12:01am on Friday, September 11 until 11:59pm on October 6.

"Everyone travels for free until this dispute's resolved," Mr Garrett said.

"This is a decision that's been made because we can't get Transdev Sydney Ferries and their parent company, Transdev Australasia, to the table for a fair wage increase.

" We've been trying now 13 odd times with meetings. Workers have had enough. "

Transport for NSW says Manly services have been disrupted due to a limited ban on overtime work. (ABC News)

Mr Garrett said Transdev had made an offer of a 3.3 per cent wage increase per year, which he described as "substandard".

702 ABC Sydney has contacted Transdev for comment.

Mr Garrett said some services might be cancelled as a result of industrial action banning some overtime work on ferries.

"Part of the problem with these negotiations is that workers have got to work endless overtime to keep services running," Mr Garrett said.

"Our intention is not to stop the services. We're not taking strike action."

The Maritime Union of Australia says ferry workers "have had enough". (ABC News)

Sydney's ferries were impacted on Wednesday morning last week due to a stop-work meeting of union members.

Deactivating readers falls outside industrial action: Transdev

Despite the union's announcement, Transport for NSW said normal fares would continue to apply on Sydney Ferries services.

According to a statement from Transport for NSW, Transdev Sydney Ferries considered deactivating Opal readers as being outside of the industrial action notified by the maritime union.

"There has been some speculation about free travel on Sydney Ferries during this period," Transport for NSW coordinator-general Howard Collins said.

" However, normal fares continue to apply and all passengers are required to tap on and tap off with a valid Opal card or contactless payment method when travelling. "

However, Mr Garrett said the union would be going ahead with the industrial action as announced.

"We won't be selling, collecting or validating tickets," Mr Garrett said.

"Passengers I'm sure will be enjoying a free ferry trip as from Friday."

Mr Collins told 702 ABC Sydney on Tuesday that the Manly ferry service was experiencing significant disruptions from the union's industrial action on overtime work.

"We're asking customers if they're travelling by ferry, or planning to, check in advance," Mr Collins said.

"We are now asking Transdev to focus on maintaining those core routes."

title: 'Never nasty, always naughty': Blanche d'Alpuget was far more than just Bob Hawke's wife
text:
To be the subject of one of Blanche d'Alpuget's biographical works was to be seen and known completely, warts and all.

Industrial arbitrator Sir Richard Kirby likened the experience of reading the biographer's musings of him to being caught in the nude.

Her future husband and political giant Bob Hawke described some of the images d'Alpuget had captured in her landmark biography of him as "grotesque".

D'Alpuget was an acclaimed author of biographies, novels and essays. (ABC News)

Her biographies of Mr Hawke were among her most well-known works but d'Alpuget, who died on Wednesday, refused to be known only as the former prime minister's second wife.

"I had my own sense of who I was and what I'd done, and I'd had a career before him," she told ABC's 7.30 following Mr Hawke's 2019 death.

It was her strong sense of self that allowed her to weather the torrent of hostility that came her way after her love affair with the former prime minister became known.

"As for people disapproving of me, I figured that was their problem. They were acting in prejudice and ignorance," she told ABC Nightlife in last November.

"If you're very in love with somebody, that love so enhances your life and your attitude, that negativity doesn't have much chance of getting a foothold."

A political scandal

The pair first met in 1970 in Jakarta, where d'Alpuget had been living with her first husband, Anthony Pratt.

d'Alpuget and Mr Hawke were criticised over their love affair. (Verity Chambers, Newspix)

Though his prime ministership was still more than a decade away, Mr Hawke had already made a name for himself during the union movement, but he had been an unknown to d'Alpuget.

"I'd been living overseas for nine years … I didn't know who the hell he was," she told the ABC's Conversation Hour.

" But I found him very, very interesting and, more to the point, a man of extremely good character. "

They met again some six years later when d'Alpuget was working on her biography of Sir Richard Kirby, with the writer admitting there was an "energy" between them while Mr Hawke was still married to first wife, Hazel.

"Neither of us said a thing about it … we knew we would become lovers that night," she told ABC's The Conversation Hour.

She said she "used to feel very sad for Hazel" after Mr Hawke divorced her.

Correcting the record

Decades after the Hawke biography was first published, d'Alpuget returned to her seminal work in 2019 with the aim of setting the record straight about Mr Hawke's relationship with political partner turned rival, former prime minister Paul Keating.

"There was a titanic struggle for the prime ministership, but beneath it, not dead but in hibernation, a profound respect and admiration lived on between them," d'Alpuget wrote in the updated biography.

She admitted she had been among those who believed a "warped depiction" of the pair's relationship in the lead up to and the aftermath of Mr Keating successfully challenging Mr Hawke's leadership.

D’Alpuget at the Bob Hawke Beer and Leisure Centre in Sydney in 2022. (AAP: Paul Braven)

"I didn't believe my husband. I think a wife who believes her husband all the time is a very unwise woman," she told The Conversation Hour.

D'Alpuget's body of work outside her political biographies was an eclectic one, covering everything from essays exploring love and lust to meticulously researched historical fiction.

She said her fictional characters were as real to her as any of her other writing subjects.

"I used to just see them in front of me… they were like people I knew intensely well," she told ABC Overnights.

d'Alpuget first met Mr Hawke in Jakarta in 1970. (AAP: Dean Lewis)

But there were some subjects d'Alpuget refused to touch.

"I did think of writing about [King] Richard [I of England] and I did quite a lot of research and read about the Third Crusade. I just don't like him," she said.

"It helps [to like the subject] because you live with them so much."

A portrait of death

Few biographers are present for their subject's death, but d'Alpuget was holding Mr Hawke's hand when he died, some 40 years since they sat down for their first interview.

Former prime minister Bob Hawke and his wife Blanche d'Alpuget arrive for his 80th birthday celebrations at the Sydney Opera House, Wednesday, December 9, 2009. (AAP: Sergio Dionisio)

In the updated biography, d'Alpuget brings readers into the room where Mr Hawke breathed his last.

"Hawke was in a deep morphine sleep. Pneumonia laboured his breathing. He would take a breath, then pause: was it his last?" she wrote.

"Suddenly, it seemed an invisible light filled the air around him and an inaudible whoosh issued with another ragged breath.

"With astonishment, the three of us [in the room] felt intense, uplifting joy."

'Never nasty, always naughty'

A number of made-for-television films have been made about Mr Hawke and d'Alpuget, one which the latter remembers as a "frightful" depiction.

"I hated it," she told the ABC.

" They had a prurient take of everything. So much nonsense is written about one … it just all merges into one great phantasmagoria. "

Ms d'Alpuget refused to write her own autobiography. (AAP: Tracey Nearmy)

D'Alpuget refused to write her own memoirs, instead appointing author Derek Riley to complete the task, as he had previously done for Mr Hawke.

Author Blanche d'Alpuget dies at 82 The family of Blanche d'Alpuget shared her final message in announcing her death.

Among those interviewed for the biography Fridays with Blanche included her stepdaughter Sue Pieters-Hawke who said Ms d'Alpuget was "never nasty" but "always naughty".

d'Alpuget muses on her mortality briefly in the biography, saying her headstone was already next to Mr Hawke's and she wanted her casket to be red on the inside and blue and white on the outside.

"She couldn't care less about who speaks [at the funeral] and says they can say anything they want, good, bad, whatever, but, with laughter, warns, 'I'll be listening'," Mr Riley wrote.

title: Communities in Victoria's west push for return of passenger trains
text:
Regional Victorian residents and public transport advocates are pushing for the return of passenger rail services along crucial routes in the state, as it heads towards the November election.

Two of Victoria's largest regional cities, Geelong and Ballarat, have had no rail connection for nearly five decades, while Mildura in Victoria's north-west has been without a passenger rail service since 1993 when the Kennett government discontinued the service.

For years, residents along the Geelong-Ballarat route, which is currently only used for freight, have called for the return of passenger rail services, with those calls backed by the Victorian Greens.

Deputy leader of the Greens and MP for western Victoria, Sarah Mansfield, said "it's time to open a conversation" about reinstating the service.

"A lot of people actually do travel between the two places, but they have to rely on a car," she said.

The other options are buses, with three daily services between Geelong and Ballarat, or catching a train into Melbourne first, but Dr Mansfield said "you're looking at several hours each way".

"It's no wonder people end up resorting to using their cars," she said.

There are growing calls for the restoration of passenger rail services between Geelong and Ballarat. (ABC News)

Dr Mansfield said there was high demand for a Geelong-Ballarat service due to significant growth in the area, which she said was only set to increase more in the coming decades.

"As Geelong and Ballarat become more significant economic and educational centres in and of themselves, there is more interest in people being able to travel between the two," she said.

The Greens hope to connect the route with the Maryborough to Ballarat line.

Wimmera Mallee left behind

Meanwhile, in Victoria's north-west, Mildura remains the largest regional city in the state without access to a passenger rail service.

Currently, the nearest passenger train service is based in Swan Hill, two and a half hours away, with passengers required to catch a coach service from Mildura to Swan Hill.

Alternatively, residents can take the overnight bus to Melbourne, but both options take about eight hours each way.

Passengers wait at the Mildura bus station, hoping to get a seat on a 3:55am coach to Swan Hill. (ABC News: Grace Marshall)

A growing number of residents are calling for a train service between Mildura and Maryborough, which would connect to the wider rail network.

Rail Revival Alliance president Noel Laidlaw said costs of airfares, an aging population and the state of the roads between Mildura and Melbourne meant public transport was the only viable option for many.

"If [people] want to go and see grandkids or go to the doctors or whatever, and they've got to go to Melbourne, they might not have the $700 to fork out for the flight," Mr Laidlaw said.

Mildura Rural City Council is one of the five councils along the potential route which are advocating for the reintroduction of the service.

Council said the region faced significant challenges due to the absence of passenger trains, with the region's remoteness and limited public transport options restricting residents' access to essential services, education and social opportunities in other Victorian towns and in Melbourne.

Similar calls for the return of passenger rail have been echoed in the Wimmera, where the V/Line train service was discontinued in 1993.

The V/Line passenger rail service to Horsham ceased in 1993. (ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya)

The Melbourne to Adelaide train, The Overland, stops at stations across the Wimmera region four times a week: twice as it heads to Adelaide and twice when it comes back to Melbourne.

It has no mid-week service.

The train also goes on a standard gauge line via Ararat and Geelong, bypassing Ballarat, where many residents need to travel for medical appointments and other services.

Nhill resident Margaret Millington is one of many people in the Wimmera who travels to Ballarat and Melbourne for medical appointments and to see family.

"The services that we are offered in Nhill, Horsham and the other regions along the way are just so inadequate, especially for disabled people, for families and the elderly," she said.

Margaret Millington is one of many Wimmera residents calling for more frequent coach services. (ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya)

Ms Millington said in communities like Nhill, aging residents have to rely on others to transport them to places they need to go.

A V/Line coach currently runs from Nhill to Ararat via Horsham, connecting with the wider train network at Ararat, but locals, including Ms Millington, are pushing for more frequent coach services to meet their daily needs.

They want to couple this with an additional mid-week Overland service in the short term, and in the longer term, the return of the V/Line train.

"That could happen now, and down the track, perhaps they could look at having daily services extended on from Ararat to Nhill … and with more than one service a week, with many services," Ms Millington said.

She recommended the state government do a feasibility study into how viable the passenger train would be for the Wimmera.

Questions about viability

Currently, the V/Line train servicing the Wimmera and Mallee ceases at Ararat and Maryborough.

The tracks beyond both stations were reconverted to standard gauge lines following the discontinuation of passenger rail, to focus on freight.

It means the lines are too narrow for current V/Line trains, which run on broad-gauge tracks across the state.

Trains cannot currently travel past Ararat directly to Melbourne, but must instead go via Geelong if they leave Horsham, Stawell or Nhill. (Supplied: Mark Radford)

RMIT University sustainability and urban planning lecturer Liam Davies said if passenger rail was to be reinstated to Horsham and Mildura, a shuttle service to and from Ararat and Maryborough to connect with the wider rail network would be the "quickest and easiest option".

In 2022, the Parliamentary Budget Office estimated that a passenger rail to Mildura running three times a week would cost $47 million.

Dr Davies said the figure would have considered the cost to upgrade the railway stations to be able to accommodate passenger rail and to modify the V/Line trains to be able to run on standard gauge.

He estimated that number would have increased since the 2022 forecast, but not by a lot.

"[It] is reasonably simple and probably reasonably doable within a modest budget," Dr Davies said.

However, he said the track would be limited to 80 kilometres an hour, meaning it would still take longer than the current service.

He believed the best option for the Wimmera in the short term would be to increase frequency of The Overland to service the region.

"That would then complement the existing coaches that run between Horsham and Ararat that connect in with the rest of the V/Line passenger network," Dr Davies said.

Liam Davies says the break in gauge is the biggest issue with reinstating passenger rail to Mildura and Horsham. (ABC News: Nicholas Mc Elroy)

Parties respond to calls

Jeff Moran, a former Department of Transport worker and now policy coordinator with the Greens Ballarat branch and a preselected Greens candidate for the seat of Lowan in western Victoria, said that, if elected, he would push for a shuttle train service between Kaniva and Ararat, that would run three times a day.

"[That would cost] next to nothing," Mr Moran said.

" There is already a passenger rail service there, there are already stations there, the infrastructure's all there, it's just about putting trains and train crews on. "

Mr Moran estimated the revival of a Ballarat to Geelong service would cost about $800 million, mainly for level crossing and platform upgrades and a fleet of trains.

Residents in the Wimmera and the Mallee are advocating for the return of passenger rail services. (Supplied: Victorian Department of Transport)

One Nation member for the northern Victoria region Rikki-Lee Tyrell said the party supported the reintroduction of passenger rail services to Mildura, but said an audit of the Treasury would be required to see what money is available.

Speaking with ABC Regional Drive earlier this month, Shadow Minister for Public Transport Matthew Guy said he understood the desire from communities in western and north-west Victoria to be better connected by passenger rail.

He said Labor was "looking closely at the case for returning passenger rail services to Mildura and increasing services to Horsham" and would "work through these options" as part of its broader transport policy.

Mr Guy said the opposition would have more to say about passenger rail services in the Wimmera Mallee before the election.

In a statement, the state government said it was continuing to deliver more coach services across regional Victoria and would always ensure communities in the west and north-west Victoria had affordable and reliable public transport options.

title: Tears flow as tennis star lets two-set lead slip in first major quarterfinal
text:
Frances Tiafoe has cut short his celebration to console friendly rival Alex Michelsen after coming back from two sets down to reach the US Open semifinals for the third time.

The 11th seed recovered time and time again to beat Michelsen 5-7, ​3-6, 7-5, 6-3, 7-6(10/6) and end the 22-year-old's first trip past the second round at his home slam.

Unseeded world number 46 Michelsen, whose previous best at a grand slam was a fourth-round berth at the 2025 Australian Open, was up a break in the third set and served for the match at 5-4 but Tiafoe won seven straight games to stay alive and take a commanding lead in the fourth frame.

Michelsen refused to go away though, taking a 3-0 in the decider, only for Tiafoe to once again storm back and take the set in a 10-point tiebreak.

After drilling a forehand passing shot down the line to secure the win after four hours and 38 minutes, Tiafoe began to celebrate his great escape before cutting his elation short to embrace his compatriot, who cried into his shoulder.

"As soon as I hugged him I saw he was crying already," Tiafoe told ESPN.

"I was like 'Man I know. I've been there twice, lost in five.' … He's young and he hasn't been there.

"We're super tight. We've always had a great relationship. We laugh and joke all the time. He's one of my good buddies on tour.

"I know how much that hurts. I know how much he wanted that today. It's something that you dream about.

"I just told him, 'You're going to be here so many more times, man. And I'm going to be in a rocking chair when you do.'"

Tiafoe appeared to have lost all the magic of his early campaign before ​wresting the momentum in ‌the third set and clinching it with a forehand winner to the deafening cheers of the fans at Arthur Ashe Stadium.

Michelsen had flown under the radar in his deepest major run but ‌he earned respect on the biggest stage of American tennis with 21 aces and 55 winners against Tiafoe, although he counted the cost of 61 unforced errors in the marathon match.

"I slowly, slowly started ​getting my rhythm there," ‌said Tiafoe, who will next play either eighth seed Ben Shelton or defending champion Carlos Alcaraz.

"He's a hell of a player. I mean, he easily could have won today."

Michelsen said after his fourth-round victory that he had improved and would try to change things, but was glad to have shared the court with a friend.

"I was trying to keep it together and I didn't do a good job of that," Michelsen said.

"He's also an unbelievable guy and a very good friend of mine," he added.

Michelsen left the court with a towel on his head, raising his arm to acknowledge the cheers from the crowd.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

Reuters/AP

title: Made for $1,500, this Australian film takes a swipe at greedy landlords
text:
If you had told Connor van Helsing when he was homeless that one day he would star in a movie about his experience he wouldn't have believed you.

Fast facts about About the Soufflé What: A very Darwin story by way of Jean-Luc Godard and the French New Wave Directed by: Jacob Hazeldine Starring: Connor van Helsing, Jesse Milne, Michael van Berkel When: Screening at the Darwin International Film Festival, September 11 Likely to make you feel: Like housing is a human right, not the whim of the rich

"It's indescribable," he says, as he reflects on the times he struggled to find a place to sleep. His experiences are the basis of the film About the Soufflé, which will have its world premiere this week at the Darwin International Film Festival.

Having been homeless three times, things got pretty grim for van Helsing, who once inspected a rental that turned out to be a shipping container.

"It's a crisis, that's for sure," van Helsing says.

"With the complete lack of rental rights, [landlords] are leasing anything and not taking care of it at all, just to rob you at the end of your tenancy, anyway."

Homelessness isn't just about sleeping rough. Van Helsing has also endured extended stretches of insecure couch-surfing, relying on the generosity of mates; an increasingly common occurrence that masks the extent of the crisis.

"It's not just about being at the bottom of the barrel," van Helsing adds. "It's way more common than you might think."

Actor Connor van Helsing brings a lived experience of homelessness to About The Soufflé. (Supplied: Darwin International Film Festival)

Sobering numbers

The stats back van Helsing up. Forget getting a foothold on the property ladder; even just renting is increasingly out of reach for many Australians. A new report by the NT Council of Social Services (NTCSS) shows at the end of 2025, the Northern Territory had the second highest average rent in the country behind NSW.

Cost-of-living pressure 'entrenching disadvantage' in the NT The NT has the second highest rent in the country, with households having to set aside more of their weekly wages to cover essential costs.

The report also found that of the rentals listed in the NT, none were affordable for a single person on minimum wage, JobSeeker, Youth Allowance, the Disability Support or Age Pension.

It's why emerging filmmaker Jacob Hazeldine, 25, made About the Soufflé.

Shot for an astonishing $1,500 and relying on a volunteer village of mostly non-professionals, his debut feature draws on the lived experiences of van Helsing — who co-wrote the film — and their inner circle, including van Helsing's co-star, Jesse Milne.

"I was pretty confronted by the toll homelessness was having on them," Hazeldine says.

"I saw it as a potential avenue to create a circuit breaker in this cycle that Connor was in. To allow him some agency, with the added benefit of creating a film that provides insight into a lot of real stuff."

Jacob Hazeldine saw the effects of the Northern Territory's housing crisis first-hand. (Supplied: Darwin International Film Festival)

Hazeldine previously worked as a project officer at the NTCSS. "We were representing bodies that look after people who are going through housing difficulties," he says.

"It's increasingly the norm. Not something that raises eyebrows, which is pretty sad."

About the Soufflé was a game-changer for van Helsing.

He plays Connor, a character not unlike himself who's sleeping in a garage on a suburban property in Darwin. Connor's rudely awoken one morning by his live-in landlord (played by Michael van Berkel, who also did a crash course in sound-recording for the film) who evicts him without notice.

This crisis sparks a funny and occasionally freaky odyssey, as Connor hunts for a place to live, a gig to pay the rent (reluctantly) and some dope to smoke (less reluctantly).

Deckchairs and dollars

Shot predominantly in black and white by cinematographer Mitch Drescher, About the Soufflé embraces both visual and thematic nods towards Breathless, the similarly edgy and inventive debut feature of French critic-turned-filmmaker Jean-Luc Godard that was also shot on the hop with a small handheld camera.

Loading Instagram content

The name is a knowing wink to the French title of Godard's film, À bout de souffle.

"I was exposed to Breathless at film school, learning how they made it," Hazeldine says.

"These new, pocket-sized cameras we have access to are really democratising filmmaking. We're seeing the parallels between what we're doing and the French New Wave, leveraging it to create something sincere and authentic."

That authenticity, and the film's fearlessness in tackling one of Australia's most pressing crises, is a breath of fresh air, and one that caught the attention of the DIFF programmers.

Hazeldine couldn't believe it when they called, wanting to screen About the Soufflé at Darwin's iconic Deckchair Cinema.

"I'm really proud of the film, and I'm so happy that we're able to premiere it at such a great venue with an understanding audience," Hazeldine says.

"It's so validating, that we created something of merit, after the culmination of so much work and with such little ingress, having tried to get money from Screen Australia and Screen Territory and got nowhere."

That necessitated some nifty solutions, including Hazeldine composing the film's hectic score on a Nintendo Switch.

"There's a $15 app which lets you emulate all of these Korg synthesizers," he reveals. "So that's how we built the sonic landscape."

Movies matter

Van Helsing reckons the rise of unique Australian cinematic voices that make-do-and-mend is at least in part because they insist on doing it their own way without interference.

"There's a burgeoning anti-tech, anti-corporation sentiment among a lot of youngsters that makes them shy away from the mainstream, even if they could access it," he says.

" There's just such a rejection of these big faceless entities. Like, why bring that into yourself? You've got mates, a camera and skills. Just f***ing do it. "

Jacob Hazeldine's miniscule cast and crew shot for just 17 days to make About the Soufflé. (Supplied: Instagram)

Hazeldine agrees: "Looking back on it, this film has no right to exist. It's a Jenga tower held together with hopes and dreams where every element had to fall into place. We were shooting for two and a half weeks straight, and if something fell through at any moment, it would have cascaded and destroyed the whole thing."

About the Soufflé was too important a story to tell for it to fall flat at the final hurdle, in a town Hazeldine suggests cares more about accommodating the American military complex than those experiencing or at risk of homelessness.

"We've got a cultural schism up here, with a really radical right-wing invasion, over the last few years, bulldozing significant bushland to build all these suburbs and gerrymander our electorates," Hazeldine says.

"There's not a lot of love for homeless people and those living in poverty.

"It's cooked."

About the Soufflé screens at the Darwin International Film Festival on September 11.

title: Sydney's busiest emergency departments revealed in new health data
text:
South Western Sydney Local Health District is doing the heavy lifting across the city's hospitals in a range of categories, new public health data reveals.

The latest Healthcare Quarterly data from April to June 2026, released by the Bureau of Health Information (BHI), paints a picture of NSW's health system.

Overall for NSW, more elective surgery procedures were performed on time and more emergency department patients were treated on time compared with the same quarter a year earlier.

But demand across the state's hospitals remained ever-present.

The median time from arrival to leaving the emergency department for all NSW patients was 3 hours and 49 minutes, up 5 minutes compared with the same quarter a year earlier.

Sydney's busiest emergency departments

Royal North Shore Hospital had high attendance numbers. (ABC News: Heath McPherson)

The data captured emergency department attendance.

In Sydney's north, Royal North Shore Hospital had 22,805 attendances, Hornsby Ku-ring-gai Hospital had 13,153 attendances and Ryde Hospital was the lowest at 6,954.

Northern Beaches Hospital recorded 16,009 attendances, but this hospital only transitioned into the public system from April 29, so any results prior to this date cover publicly contracted services only.

Northern Beaches Hospital was also considerably busy. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

In the south-west, Liverpool Hospital had the greatest attendances at 23,773, followed closely by Campbelltown Hospital at 23,664.

The lowest rates in this local health district were Camden Hospital (3,014) and Fairfield Hospital (9,099).

Other particularly busy Sydney hospitals included St George Hospital at 21,038 attendances, and Royal Prince Alfred Hospital at 20,832.

What the data shows is the high demand faced by the South Western Sydney Local Health District, which covers an area of 6,243 square kilometres from Bankstown to Bowral.

Treatment times at Sydney hospitals

As for the percentage of patients starting treatments on time at Sydney hospital emergency departments between April to June 2026, the data showed major improvement in one key local health district.

At Liverpool Hospital, 77.5 per cent of patients started treatment on time, a 7.8 per cent increase compared to the previous year's reporting period.

The data showed treatment time improvement at Liverpool Hospital. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

Campbelltown Hospital saw one of the biggest improvements, from 53.8 per cent between April to June 2025, to 68.2 per cent in this year's period.

Camden Hospital recorded 84.1 per cent for the 2026 reporting period, Ryde Hospital had 83.5 per cent and Royal North Shore Hospital was 74.6 per cent.

As for the lesser performing hospitals in this category, Fairfield Hospital stood at 49 per cent, and Prince of Wales Hospital was 52.6 per cent.

Blacktown Hospital was also one of the lower rates at 49 per cent, though it was a 9.3 per cent improvement from the previous year's period.

Health Minister Ryan Park acknowledged there was "still a lot to do in our emergency departments".

When asked on 702 ABC Sydney about one caller's experience of waiting 20 hours at Westmead Hospital, Mr Park said it was "not good enough".

"But one of the challenges is … there has been a massive increase and nearly doubling of the patients that are categorised two and three," Mr Park said in reference to the past 15 years in NSW.

Category two refers to emergency cases, and category three refers to urgent cases.

"They're the sickest patients in the system. They need to spend more time in an emergency department," he said.

Episodes of mental health care at Sydney hospitals

Royal Prince Alfred Hospital saw a high number of mental health care cases. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Patients admitted for mental health episodes of care at Sydney hospitals were also recorded.

The inner west saw great demand, with Royal Prince Alfred Hospital having one of the highest rates at 690 episodes, along with Concord Hospital at 529.

The city's south-west also did heavy lifting at Campbelltown Hospital (532), Liverpool Hospital (382) and Nepean Hospital (345).

Elective surgeries at Sydney hospitals

Across NSW in the reporting period, 85.6 per cent of elective surgeries were performed on time, not including the Hunter New England Local Health District, as centralised data from this district was not available for the report.

There were 697 NSW patients on the waiting list that had waited longer than clinically recommended.

As for Sydney specifically, only a few hospitals recorded considerable rates of patients waiting longer than recommended for surgery at the end of the quarter.

At Prince of Wales Hospital, 71 patients waited longer than recommended. (ABC Radio Sydney: Declan Bowring)

Prince of Wales Hospital recorded 71 patients waiting longer than recommended and St George Hospital had 49.

Mr Park said the system was under pressure from 1,300 beds being taken up every day from people who were medically fine but waiting on NDIS or aged care spaces.

"That's the equivalent of two Sydney hospitals not to be used," he said.

title: How Ned overcame a decade of pain to return to running
text:
The doubts that occasionally flit across Ned Buckell's mind are likely to be familiar to runners whatever standard they're at.

Buckell's story is different to most, though.

A life-threatening infection as a teenager.

A year-and-a-half on crutches.

Another serious infection just when it felt like things were on track, resulting in a hip replacement before he was 21.

And a race number from the 2016 Melbourne Marathon Festival pinned to his wall, reminding him that there is still a destination to reach despite the darkness.

"There's definitely been times when you think to yourself, what am I doing this for?" Buckell tells ABC Sport.

"Why am I still trying to get back running at a reasonably high level?

"I think the biggest thing is because I knew I would do it.

"Those thoughts always creep into my mind like, 'Why am I still going? You're not going to get the most out of it,' but I can get the most out of what I can, and I've always told myself I can.

"That's probably why I haven't given up.

"Even though there've been countless times when you want to, when you keep getting struck down, there are signs, and the universe is telling you to stop.

"You have to just sort of not ignore them, but just push them aside and prove that it's not."

'If it had gone any further, then that would have been the end of me'

Running was Ned Buckell's life. After his injury and illness, it still is. (Supplied: 2045)

Buckell was always going to be a runner.

His dad, John, was a runner and both Ned and his twin brother, Matt, would tag along to cross-country races around Bendigo and run from the age of five.

Theirs was an early introduction to the lung-busting freedom that a pair of trainers and the open trails of the countryside can afford.

"Me, my twin brother and my two older brothers were all always very competitive," Buckell says.

"That turned us into sporty individuals that always want to be better than each other.

"I've always been a runner, but it wasn't until maybe 14 or maybe 13 where I quit footy and was trying to focus on it a bit more.

"I knew me and my brother had some sort of talent, that we could take it to the next level.

"My twin brother has done that, but I haven't. I've just been struck down with this, really."

Sometimes you have to really love running to get up in the freezing cold of winter. (Supplied: 2045)

Buckell's issues all stem back to an infection he got when he was 14 years old, just after he turned to running seriously.

"The night it all happened, I was playing basketball with my mates at his house," Buckell recalls.

"It was a warm September night, the boys were in shorts and T-shirts, and I was in trackies and a hoodie, I was getting these fevers.

"We were all thinking that something's not right, so I rode home with Matt and then the fevers got really bad."

Buckell's parents were away, so it was up to his Nan and Pop to take him to the local GP, who initially diagnosed a twisting hernia, with Buckell struggling to stand due to the pain.

The GP sent Ned to a specialist, who instantly transferred him to the emergency department, where the scale of Buckell's issue became terrifyingly clear.

A staph infection had entered Ned's hip, driving up his temperature to dangerous levels.

"I ended up getting four hip washouts; three in Bendigo, which had no effect, basically, and then they sent me to the Royal Children's Hospital for another one," Buckell says.

The then-14-year-old spent the next three-and-a-half weeks in hospital, fortunate to be alive.

"I was on the cardiac ward because the infection had spread to my heart," Buckell explains.

"If it had gone any further, then that would have been the end of me.

"I never realised how severe it was, probably until now that I've finished my degree."

'Sometimes it's impossible to see that light'

Ned Buckell says the support of his family was essential. (Supplied: 2045)

Ned was discharged from hospital just in time to celebrate his 15th birthday.

It was a bittersweet moment.

The teenager spent the next 18 months on crutches, "torture" for a kid who described himself as "one of the most active that you'd meet".

"There were times that I, you know, I'm very lucky that I've had a supportive family," Ned says, understandably struggling to find the words to recall what had been a horrendous time.

"If I hadn't had that support around me, I definitely wouldn't be here today.

"There were times when you just wanted a way out.

"I knew that I couldn't do that, but watching all my brothers start work, play their sports … I was never jealous, but I was so sad all the time about missing out.

"It was extremely tough. You wouldn't wish that upon anyone, really."

Buckell says he gets goosebumps talking about this period of his life, underlining what a tough topic it is to address even 10 years on.

But despite all the darkness, Ned says that he always kept an optimistic mindset, something which he knows helped him a lot.

"It has been pretty important just to try to find the good in things," Buckell says.

"It's a hard topic for me to talk about, but it's something that I've acknowledged, and I'm just grateful to be where I'm at right now, to be honest.

"I know everyone battles their own shit, and I think the way I've looked at it all is there's always a light at the end of the tunnel.

"And sometimes it's impossible to see that light. And sometimes it's not there.

"But you just have to keep going forward and pushing through.

"It's hard, but I think talking about it does help me try to word things a little bit better."

Running is 'just something I do'

Ned Buckell has had to deal with serious illness and a traumatic injury, but has found peace in running. (Supplied: 2045)

The positivity was tested in 2022 when, having fought his way back to a high level, running 14:42 at the Bendigo 5km Frenzy to break a local under-20 record, his hip started playing up again.

He was diagnosed with avascular necrosis, the death of bone tissue due to a lack of blood flow.
